value: /sorted, mid-voyage of emit-refuses-an-uncleared-crossing — its chart's validate criterion 7 demands this debt be FILED rather than absorbed, and re-sealing the corpus inside a gate ticket is exactly the absorption that criterion refuses.

P2 — P2 because the state has exactly one consumer today (clearance.py's proven-space refusal) and the voyage that gave it that consumer routed around the debt honestly — by scoping the demanded set to the crossing into a rest, which /sail seals one step earlier, rather than by widening a roster. So nothing is currently blocked. It is not P3 because the number is 6 of 78 and the mechanism is now load-bearing on every crossing into proven-space: the first component that needs to cross and finds its seal decayed pays a re-seal errand, and falsifier clause (4) of the parent ticket names exactly that as a real red. CHILD (b) IS NOT P2 — four seal trails failing INTEGRITY is a Law 7 problem and should be looked at on its own clock.

value.a: Two assumptions were load-bearing and are now named. (1) THAT A GREEN SEAL MEANS PROVEN — it does not, and that is the design working: validation_store.standing() re-reads the source fingerprint the tester recorded, so a seal green on code that has since moved refuses. Measured 2026-08-10 across the corpus: 6 of 78 proofs stand in proven-space, and 4 of the 6 were sealed in the last hour by the voyage doing the measuring. Nearly the whole corpus is green-by-seal and red-by-fingerprint at once. (2) THAT THE FIX IS A RE-SEAL SWEEP — this is the assumption to kill loudly. Re-sealing 72 proofs in one act would put the whole corpus in proven-space for exactly as long as nobody edits anything, which is minutes; the number would be a snapshot of when the sweep ran, not a property of the corpus. What is actually unknown is whether proven-space is meant to be a state the corpus RESTS in or a state a component enters at the moment it needs to be leaned on. This ticket exists to settle that question first, and the sweep is downstream of the answer, not a substitute for it.

Two points I would have asserted wrapped and have not. (a) THE FOUR BROKEN SEAL TRAILS ARE A DIFFERENT DEFECT and are not counted in the 72. cairn/devices/inference_domain/validations/ carries four proofs whose failure is 'the seal trail ... ' — a TRAIL INTEGRITY refusal, not a stale fingerprint, which means the append-only chain itself does not verify. That is a Law 7 record-of-truth problem and it is louder than staleness; it is child (b) and it is the one to look at first. (b) WHAT PROVEN-SPACE IS FOR is genuinely open. Today exactly one consumer reads it — clearance.py's second refusal — so 'the corpus is out of proven-space' has one observable consequence: a crossing cannot be cleared onto a component whose seal has decayed. Whether that is a problem or the mechanism working correctly depends on the answer to the assumption above, and asserting it wrapped would be designing for a problem nobody has.

No exclusive-and-terminal collision; the congruency lab was recompiled and consulted 2026-08-10 before this cast, and no intention claims authority over what proven-space is for — cairn/devices/tester's charter owns the seal and the horizon, and this node is a question about the STATE those produce, so it berths under the tester rather than beside it. Two distinctions to record. (1) tickets/emit-refuses-an-uncleared-crossing (in flight, at WATCHME) is where this was measured, and it is the ticket that gave proven-space its first real consumer. Their whys are opposed only in appearance: that ticket needed the demanded set narrow enough that the corpus's staleness did not refuse the fleet, and it got there by scoping rather than by re-sealing — deliberately leaving this debt whole and filed rather than absorbing it. (2) cairn/devices/tester's own horizon already contemplates seal decay; this is not a second opinion about that, it is the corpus-wide COUNT the horizon never had, and the count is what makes the question answerable.
